questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: identify the components that produce a fiscal deficit
questions.stem: Government purchases are 300 billion units, taxes are 250 billion, transfers are 40 billion and net exports are zero. What is the government's budget balance?

options.text: A deficit of 90 billion, because purchases plus transfers of 340 billion exceed tax revenue of 250 billion
A surplus of 50 billion, because tax revenue of 250 exceeds purchases of 300 net of nothing
options.misconception: compares tax revenue with purchases alone and ignores transfers

options.text: A deficit of 50 billion, because it takes 300 minus 250 and stops there
options.misconception: leaves transfers out of the government's outlays

options.text: A deficit of 340 billion, because total spending is the whole of the deficit
options.misconception: treats the entire level of spending as the borrowing requirement

questions.explanation: The budget balance is tax revenue less government purchases less transfers, so 250 minus 300 minus 40 gives minus 90 billion, a deficit of 90. Transfers are part of government outlays even though they are not purchases of goods and services, which is the step that produces the 50 figure, and a surplus of 50 requires comparing 250 against 300 alone, which ignores the payment entirely. The deficit is the difference between the two flows, not the size of either, and net exports at zero means the government deficit is the whole of the economy's net borrowing.
questions.hint: Subtract both purchases and transfers from tax revenue.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: distinguish the actual deficit from the cyclically adjusted deficit
questions.stem: A country's government runs a deficit of 40 billion units in a year when output is 5 percent below its full-employment level. What does the cyclically adjusted deficit do?

options.text: It removes the revenue and spending that the output gap caused, so it measures the deficit the budget would show at full employment
It adds back the lost tax revenue, so it always shows a larger deficit than the actual one
options.misconception: assumes every output gap raises the adjusted deficit

options.text: It scales all spending and revenue up by the size of the output gap
options.misconception: inflates the whole budget by the gap rather than removing its effect

options.text: It sets the actual deficit equal to the primary surplus, ignoring the output position
options.misconception: confuses cyclical adjustment with stripping out interest payments

questions.explanation: Tax revenue falls automatically when output falls and transfers rise automatically for the same reason, so part of any measured deficit in a recession exists only because the cycle is weak. Cyclical adjustment strips those two automatic effects out, leaving the structural position: what the budget would look like at full-employment output. Since the output gap here is negative, the revenue shortfall is larger than normal, so the adjusted deficit is normally larger than the actual one, but the sign depends on the automatic stabilisers rather than on the arithmetic, and scaling the whole budget by the gap is not adjustment at all.
questions.hint: Ask which parts of the deficit would disappear if output were at its full-employment level.

questions.topic: Debt ratio and the interest-growth differential
questions.learningObjective: state what makes the debt-to-output ratio rise or fall
questions.stem: A government has debt equal to 70 percent of a year's output. The average interest rate on that debt is 4 percent a year and nominal output grows at 3 percent a year. What does the differential imply?

options.text: The interest-growth differential is positive, so the debt ratio drifts upward unless the government runs a primary surplus
The differential is positive, so the debt ratio must fall because the surplus repays some of it
options.misconception: ignores that a primary surplus is a separate decision from the differential

options.text: The differential is one percent, so the debt ratio falls by exactly one percentage point a year
options.misconception: treats the differential as the change in the ratio without a primary balance

options.text: The differential is zero, because four percent of interest is offset by three percent of growth
options.misconception: subtracts the two rates and calls the difference zero

questions.explanation: The ratio moves when the interest rate on the debt exceeds the growth rate of the denominator, because each year the stock grows by the interest bill while the output it is measured against grows more slowly. Four percent against three percent leaves a positive differential of one percentage point, so the ratio snowballs and the government must run a primary surplus of about 0.7 percent of output merely to hold the ratio at 70 percent. Calling the difference zero because the two rates are close reverses the test, and treating the ratio as falling without a surplus omits the mechanism entirely.
questions.hint: Compare the interest rate on the debt with the growth rate of output.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: define the primary balance and state why it governs the debt path
questions.stem: A government pays 90 billion units of interest and collects 800 billion of taxes while spending 700 billion excluding interest. What is its primary balance, and why is it the figure that matters?

options.text: A primary surplus of 100 billion, which is the amount left after interest to either repay or add to debt
A primary deficit of 10 billion, which is the total budget balance before transfers
options.misconception: computes the overall balance and labels it the primary one

options.text: A primary surplus of 190 billion, which adds the interest payment to the surplus
options.misconception: counts interest as a resource available for repayment

options.text: A primary surplus of 800 billion, which is tax revenue before any spending at all
options.misconception: reports gross revenue and ignores every kind of outlay

questions.explanation: The primary balance is revenue less everything except interest, so 800 minus 700 is a surplus of 100 billion, and adding back the 90 of interest gives an overall surplus of 10 billion. The primary balance governs the debt path because interest is not a discretionary decision: it is what the existing debt costs, and adding it back would double-count a payment that is already committed. The residual after interest is what the government can actually choose to use to repay or to accumulate, which is why the debt ratio's drift is set by the primary balance against the interest-growth differential.
questions.hint: Leave interest out of the outlays, and ask what is left to spend on the debt itself.

questions.topic: Fiscal multiplier and the monetary response
questions.learningObjective: explain why a fiscal multiplier depends on the monetary response
questions.stem: A government raises spending by 10 billion units in an economy where the central bank holds its interest rate and money supply fixed. What happens to the size of the multiplier?

options.text: It is smaller, because the extra spending raises interest rates, which crowds out some of the private spending it was meant to supplement
It is larger, because a fixed interest rate lets all of the extra spending reach output
options.misconception: assumes interest rates cannot move when the money supply is fixed

options.text: It is unchanged, because the multiplier depends only on the spending multiplier alone
options.misconception: ignores interest rate and crowding-out channels in the multiplier

options.text: It becomes a tax multiplier, because spending and taxes affect output identically
options.misconception: swaps the two multipliers, which have opposite signs

questions.explanation: The fiscal multiplier is not a property of spending alone: it is the net effect after every other response to the initial demand increase. With a fixed interest rate the extra spending bids up the price level and the money demand it creates pushes the rate up, the higher rate makes some planned private investment unprofitable, and part of the initial demand is crowded out, so the realised multiplier is smaller than the simple expenditure calculation implies. Saying a fixed rate lets all the spending through confuses a fixed rate with a fixed price level, and the tax multiplier has the opposite sign because a tax cut works through the same chain from the other direction.
questions.hint: Ask what the central bank does to the interest rate when spending rises.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: compare the magnitudes of the spending and tax multipliers
questions.stem: In a model where households spend three quarters of each extra unit of disposable income and 20 percent of income goes to taxes, how do the two multipliers compare?

options.text: The spending multiplier is larger in size than the tax multiplier, because part of an extra pound of spending is taxed away before it is re-spent
The two are equal in size, because both inject one unit of demand into the circular flow
options.misconception: ignores the tax leakage that applies to spending but not to a tax change

options.text: The tax multiplier is larger in size, because a tax cut reaches households with a higher propensity to spend
options.misconception: ignores that only part of the tax cut is spent rather than saved

options.text: Both are one, because the marginal propensities to spend and to save sum to one
options.misconception: mistakes the sum of the propensities for the size of a multiplier

questions.explanation: The spending multiplier is one over one minus c times one minus t, which with c of 0.75 and t of 0.20 is one over one minus 0.6, that is 2.5. The tax multiplier is minus c times one minus t over the same denominator, which is minus 0.6 over 0.4, that is minus 1.5. The spending multiplier is the larger in size because an extra unit of government purchases is taxed once before the recipients spend it, whereas an extra unit of disposable income is spent only 75 percent of the time. The signs differ as well, since a tax cut raises demand and a tax rise reduces it.
questions.hint: Both multipliers share the denominator one minus c times one minus t.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: explain why the balanced-budget multiplier is not zero
questions.stem: A government raises purchases and taxes by the same 20 billion units, with a spending multiplier of 2.5 and a tax multiplier of minus 1.5. What is the effect on output?

options.text: Output rises by 20 billion, because the larger spending multiplier outweighs the smaller tax multiplier in size
Output is unchanged, because the rise in spending is exactly matched by the rise in taxes
options.misconception: assumes the two injections are equally powerful per unit of change

options.text: Output rises by 50 billion, because only the spending increase is counted
options.misconception: applies the spending multiplier and ignores the tax increase entirely

options.text: Output falls by 30 billion, because a balanced budget is contractionary by definition
options.misconception: adds the two multiplier effects with the wrong sign on the tax term

questions.explanation: The two changes have to be added rather than set against each other: 2.5 times 20 is 50 billion of extra demand from the spending, and minus 1.5 times 20 is 30 billion of withdrawal from the taxes, and the net is 20 billion, so the balanced-budget multiplier is one, not zero. The intuition is that the tax increase destroys only part of the income it takes, since the rest is saved, so the fall in consumption is smaller than the rise in government purchases. Cancelling the two changes treats a pound of government spending and a pound of taxation as equally strong, which they are not.
questions.hint: Add the two multiplier effects; they do not have equal size.

questions.learningObjective: state the labour-supply response a supply-side tax cut assumes
questions.stem: A government cuts the top income tax rate on the argument that higher after-tax rewards will bring discouraged workers and investors back into activity. What assumption is that argument resting on?

options.text: That taxes significantly reduce the incentive to work, save and invest, so that a lower rate measurably raises the amount of labour supplied
That most people are on the top rate, so a cut reaches almost the whole workforce
options.misconception: assumes the top rate applies to the median worker rather than the top

options.text: That income tax is a large share of output, so a rate cut frees much real income
options.misconception: conflates the rate of tax with the total tax take

options.text: That the labour supply is fixed, so a lower rate raises wages and therefore output
options.misconception: holds labour supply fixed while invoking supply-side incentives

questions.explanation: A supply-side argument is a claim about the responsiveness of supply: it needs the distortion from taxation to be large enough that removing part of it changes behaviour measurably. The assumption to state is the size of the elasticity of labour supply, and the evidence on that is genuinely contested, which is why the argument is usually made as a case for a growth effect rather than a simple arithmetic one. Where a cut applies only to the top rate, the population whose incentive might change is a small share of the workforce, and the size of the rate has little to do with the size of the tax take.
questions.hint: The claim is about behaviour, so ask how much the tax distorts the choice to work.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: state what central bank independence insulates
questions.stem: A government with a large deficit wants the central bank to hold interest rates low to make the debt cheaper. What does a legally independent central bank protect against?

options.text: It insulates the interest rate decision from the fiscal pressure to monetise the deficit, preserving the credibility of the currency
It insulates the money supply from the commercial banking sector, which could otherwise create credit
options.misconception: describes the lender of last resort function rather than independence

options.text: It insulates the government's budget from the business cycle, so spending need not vary
options.misconception: claims it removes the need for automatic stabilisers in the budget

options.text: It insulates the exchange rate from the capital account, so no capital ever flows in
options.misconception: assumes independence closes the economy to international capital

questions.explanation: Independence is a commitment to set the interest rate for price stability rather than to finance the government, and what it protects is the credibility of the money: if a deficit can be met by printing, lenders will price in inflation and the real rate will not fall as the government expects. It is a constraint on the monetary authority's objectives, not a change to the way money is created, and it does nothing to stabilise the budget, which still has to respond to the cycle through automatic stabilisers. It also says nothing about the capital account, which is a question of the exchange-rate regime.
questions.hint: Ask what the authority is prevented from doing to the interest rate.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: assign the incidence of a payroll tax
questions.stem: A payroll tax of 10 percent on a wage of 40,000 units is split by law into 60 percent borne by the worker and 40 percent by the employer. Who actually bears the tax?

options.text: The economic burden depends on how elastic the supply of labour and the demand for labour are, not on how the law divides it
The worker bears 2,400 and the employer 1,600, exactly as the statute specifies
options.misconception: treats the legal split as the economic incidence

options.text: The employer bears all 4,000, because workers cannot afford to refuse the job
options.misconception: assumes labour supply is perfectly inelastic and demand is not

options.text: The worker bears all 4,000, because the worker's wage is what the law says it is
options.misconception: assumes labour demand is perfectly inelastic and supply is not

questions.explanation: The statutory split is a statement about who remits the money, not about who bears it. A payroll tax raises the cost of labour to the employer and reduces the wage the worker takes home, and the split of the burden between them is set by the relative elasticities of labour supply and labour demand in the market for that kind of work. Where supply is relatively inelastic, workers bear most of it through a smaller net wage; where demand is relatively inelastic, employers bear it through a higher labour cost. With both sides able to adjust, the burden lands in proportion to those elasticities, and the figure of 2,400 and 1,600 is only where the two elasticities happen to be equal.
questions.hint: Ask which side of the labour market can most easily change its behaviour.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: assign the incidence of a corporate tax between labour and capital
questions.stem: A country levies a corporate tax of 25 percent while capital is perfectly mobile between countries and labour is not. Where does the burden of the tax fall?

options.text: Entirely on the owners of capital, because they are the side that can move their base to another country
Split between labour and capital in proportion to their shares of national income
options.misconception: assumes both factors are equally immobile across the border

options.text: Entirely on labour, because wages are set in domestic bargaining and cannot be cut
options.misconception: reverses which of the two factors is able to leave the country

options.text: Entirely on consumers, because corporate tax is passed on in the price of goods
options.misconception: assumes perfect competition lets a tax raise the selling price

questions.explanation: Incidence follows mobility: the side that can most easily reduce its quantity in response bears more of the tax. Capital that can leave the country for a lower rate elsewhere will do so, so the tax is capitalised into a lower return on capital rather than into a higher price, and the whole 25 percent of the return is forgone by the owners of capital. Labour cannot emigrate in the same way, so it does not bear the tax. Splitting the burden by income shares would be right only if both factors were equally immobile, and a tax passed on in the price requires the firm to have the market power to raise that price.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two factors can reduce its quantity by leaving the country.

questions.learningObjective: compare a tax expenditure with direct government spending
questions.stem: A government collects 900 billion units of tax while devoting 400 billion to relieving particular kinds of income from tax. What does the 400 billion represent?

options.text: A tax expenditure, an indirect way of spending public funds that is 44.4 percent as large as direct spending of the same purpose
A direct transfer of 400 billion paid to households in cash
options.misconception: reads a tax relief as a cash payment programme

options.text: Tax revenue that the government has failed to collect through under-assessment
options.misconception: treats a deliberate relief as an administrative collection failure

options.text: A deficit of 400 billion caused by the tax relief exceeding the revenue collected
options.misconception: confuses a tax base measure with a budget shortfall

questions.explanation: Where the government chooses not to tax a base, it is spending money through the tax system rather than through a spending programme, and the result is recorded as a tax expenditure. The important difference is not the size but the visibility: an explicit spending line is debated in the budget, while relief embedded in the rates is often passed without a separate vote, which is why the two are compared at all.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: state what makes a tax progressive
questions.stem: Two households have pre-tax incomes of 20,000 and 80,000 units. The first pays 4,000 in tax and the second pays 28,000. What does this pair of figures tell you?

options.text: The average tax rate rises with income, from 20 percent to 35 percent, so the tax is progressive
The marginal tax rate rises with income, so the tax is progressive by that measure alone
options.misconception: confuses average rates with marginal rates when classifying progressivity

options.text: The tax is regressive, because the second household pays 28,000 against 4,000 in absolute terms
options.misconception: judges progressivity by absolute payments rather than by rates

options.text: The tax is proportional, because each household pays exactly one fifth of a constant share
options.misconception: reads identical proportional shares into two different average rates

questions.explanation: Progressivity is a statement about average tax rates: the household with the higher income pays the larger fraction of its income in tax, which is what the 20 percent and 35 percent figures show. Comparing the two payments in absolute terms confuses the size of the income with the size of the bill, since a progressive tax is intended to take more from the larger income. Progressivity is about averages; a marginal rate schedule is a separate object, and a schedule with rising marginal rates can still produce a flat average rate across a range of incomes.
questions.hint: Divide each tax bill by the income it was paid on.

questions.learningObjective: assess the regressivity of a consumption tax in a stated distribution
questions.stem: A 10 percent consumption tax costs the poorest household 2,000 units out of an income of 40,000 and the richest 6,000 out of 200,000. How does the tax distribute?

options.text: The tax is regressive here, taking 5 percent of the poorest income but only 3 percent of the richest
The tax is progressive here, taking 6,000 from the rich household against 2,000 from the poor one
options.misconception: compares the size of the payment rather than the share of income

options.text: The tax is proportional, since every household pays exactly 10 percent of what it spends
options.misconception: calls a constant rate on spending proportional while ignoring income shares

options.text: The tax is regressive, because the richest household pays three times the rate of the poorest
options.misconception: computes a ratio of payments in the wrong direction and calls it a rate

questions.explanation: A consumption tax is a constant rate on spending, so whether it is regressive depends on how much of income each household spends. Here the poor household spends 20,000 out of 40,000, or half its income, and pays 2,000, which is 5 percent of income; the rich household spends 60,000 out of 200,000, or 30 percent, and pays 6,000, which is 3 percent. Higher-income households save a larger share, so the same rate on spending takes a smaller share of their income. A constant rate on a quantity is not a constant rate on income, which is exactly why the classification depends on the distribution given.
questions.hint: Express each payment as a percentage of income, not of the bill.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: explain the cascading a value-added tax prevents
questions.stem: Under a sales tax, a manufacturer buys 100 of inputs, adds 40 of value, and the retailer then pays tax on the full 140. What does a value-added tax do instead?

options.text: It taxes only the value added at each stage, so the 40 is taxed once and the 100 of inputs is not taxed again
It removes the tax entirely from the intermediate input, so only the retailer pays anything
options.misconception: drops the manufacturer's liability instead of timing the tax differently

options.text: It taxes the 140 at each stage, so the same amount is taxed twice as often
options.misconception: keeps the cascading and merely changes the rate applied to it

options.text: It taxes the retail price only, so the 100 of inputs is exempt and the 140 is taxed once
options.misconception: shifts the liability to the last stage rather than taxing value added

questions.explanation: Cascading arises because a tax on the gross price of a purchase is charged again when the same value is resold, so the total tax embedded in a good rises with the number of transactions it passes through. A value-added tax credits the tax paid on inputs against the tax due on sales, which nets the tax out of the intermediate stage and leaves only the 40 of value added to be taxed at each step. The total tax on the finished good is then 40 times the rate whether it passes through one firm or five, and exempting inputs at retail instead merely relocates the liability without removing the cascade.
questions.hint: Net the tax on inputs against the tax on sales and count what is left.

questions.learningObjective: compute the deadweight cost a subsidy incurs
questions.stem: A subsidy of 10 units a unit lifts supply to 2,000 while demand at that price would be 1,600, and the trades that occur number 1,800. What is the deadweight loss?

400 units, being the number of units bought and not wanted at the subsidised price
options.misconception: reports the quantity gap and ignores the price wedge

options.misconception: multiplies by the whole gap instead of the triangle's half

Multiplying the wedge by the whole 400 gives the rectangle of the payments that were made, most of which bought units that were wanted anyway, and calling the whole 18,000 of payments deadweight confuses the cost to the treasury with the loss to society.

questions.learningObjective: state the exchange-rate channel in the tradable and non-tradable split
questions.stem: An economy's prices are split into tradable goods set at world prices and non-tradable services sold only at home. What does a rise in the price of tradables do to the two groups?

options.text: Tradable prices are pinned to world prices, so the rise falls entirely on non-tradable prices, which are where a domestic cost increase shows up
Both groups rise together, because a price rise at home reaches goods and services alike
options.misconception: assumes tradable prices are set domestically rather than in the world market

options.text: Tradable prices rise and non-tradable prices fall, since the increase frees up domestic supply
options.misconception: reverses which of the two groups the adjustment lands on

options.text: Neither group moves, because tradable prices and non-tradable prices are the same thing
options.misconception: denies the distinction between the two groups exists at all

questions.explanation: The real exchange rate is the ratio of the non-tradable price level to the world price of tradables, because tradable goods can be bought at the same price anywhere and any domestic price above that is matched by imports. A rise in tradable prices therefore cannot be absorbed domestically: it works through the exchange rate until the domestic price of tradables matches the world price again, and the adjustment falls on the non-tradable sector, whose goods cannot be imported. Treating the two groups as one, or reversing which one absorbs the shock, both miss the reason the split matters, which is the mobility of the goods across the border.
questions.hint: Ask which group can be substituted for by an import and which cannot.

questions.topic: Fixed exchange rate and monetary policy
questions.learningObjective: state what a fixed exchange rate does to monetary independence
questions.stem: A country pegs its currency to a larger economy's currency and gives up the ability to set its own interest rate. Why is that constraint unavoidable?

options.text: A fixed parity means one interest rate is consistent with the peg, so domestic policy must match the anchor country's policy
A fixed parity fixes the price level, so interest rates can still be set freely at home
options.misconception: treats a fixed currency value as a fixed domestic price level

options.text: A fixed parity removes the need for monetary policy, since trade balances adjust on their own
options.misconception: assumes the current account clears without any monetary stance

options.text: A fixed parity sets the money supply, so the government chooses its own interest rate instead
options.misconception: confuses the operation of a fixed rate with the autonomy it removes

questions.explanation: Interest parity says uncovered returns must be equal across currencies, or the peg cannot be defended against speculators who borrow in one currency and lend in the other. If the parities are fixed, that condition pins the domestic interest rate to the foreign one plus an expected depreciation, and the expected depreciation is zero when the peg holds. The country therefore gives up the interest rate as an instrument and is left with fiscal policy, which is the standard conclusion of the trilemma: peg the currency, float the interest rate, or let the capital account move, but not all three independently.
questions.hint: Interest parity ties the domestic rate to the foreign rate once the parity is fixed.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: state what a floating exchange rate permits
questions.stem: A country lets its currency float freely. What does that choice permit the monetary authority to do?

options.text: It can set its own interest rate for domestic conditions, at the cost of letting the currency absorb shocks as volatile price changes
It can set its own interest rate and keep the exchange rate stable at the same time
options.misconception: claims the two benefits are available together under a float

options.text: It must abandon control of the interest rate, since the market now sets the rate
options.misconception: confuses a floating exchange rate with a fixed one

options.text: It eliminates the need for foreign reserves, since no parity has to be defended
options.misconception: treats reserves as required only for a defended parity

questions.explanation: A float restores monetary independence, because the exchange rate is free to move instead of the interest rate, and the country can set the rate to whatever domestic conditions require. The price of that autonomy is volatility: a terms-of-trade shock or a change in foreign risk appetite is now expressed as a jump in the currency, so import prices and the domestic cost of tradables change in a way that has to be absorbed rather than defended. options.misconception: assumes inflows were a source of tax revenue rather than of credit

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.topic: Why the primary balance governs the debt path
questions.learningObjective: explain why the primary balance rather than the headline deficit sets the debt path
questions.stem: A country's deficit is 3 percent of output in a year when output is 1 percent below its full-employment level, and the government is cutting spending to bring it down. Explain why the primary balance, not the deficit, is the figure that should guide whether the debt ratio will fall.

answer.exemplar: The debt ratio next period is the ratio grossed up at the interest rate and divided by the growth of output, less the primary balance, so the only discretionary term is the primary balance. The interest bill is not a decision: it is what last year's debt already costs, and counting it in the target double-counts a payment that cannot be avoided by cutting spending this year. The output gap matters because it makes revenue lower than it would otherwise be, so part of the 3 percent deficit is cyclical and will shrink as output recovers without any further action. Cutting spending to hit a deficit target set on the headline number therefore removes demand exactly when the automatic stabilisers are already doing the stabilising, and it leaves the primary balance, which is the term that actually moves the ratio, no better than before.

questions.explanation: Ask which term in the debt equation the government can change without touching a payment already committed.
questions.hint: The trap is to treat the headline deficit as the policy variable, but the headline deficit contains a term the government cannot change this year, namely the interest on debt it issued in the past, and a term it will change by itself as output recovers. Chasing the headline number therefore means cutting spending into a gap that is closing, while the term that actually moves the debt ratio, the primary balance, is left where it was or gets worse. A deficit target can still be a useful signal about the size of the adjustment; what it cannot be is a substitute for watching the primary balance and the interest-growth differential together.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: explain why the trade balance usually worsens first after a devaluation
questions.stem: A country devalues its currency by 10 percent and then experiences a period in which the trade deficit widens before it narrows. Explain why that path is expected rather than surprising.

answer.exemplar: The devaluation raises the domestic-currency price of imports immediately, and import volumes respond only slowly because contracts, shipping and quantities already in the pipeline adjust with a lag. Spending in domestic currency on imports therefore rises first, because the price increase applies at once to every unit bought while the 4 percent volume saving has not yet arrived. Export volumes respond with the same lag, so the export side gains nothing in the first period. Later, as the volume responses arrive, the J-curve turns: if the two elasticities together exceed one, the import bill eventually rises by less than the export revenue, and the trade balance improves. The initial deterioration is thus a timing effect on the price side running ahead of the volume side, and it is strongest for a large devaluation and small elasticities.

questions.explanation: Ask which side of the trade account reacts instantly and which reacts with a lag.
questions.hint: What makes the path a curve is that the two sides of the trade account respond to different things. The devaluation changes the price of everything at once, but it changes the quantity of only what has been ordered, shipped or renegotiated, and that adjustment takes months. The price rise on imports is therefore fully in the accounts from the first day while the volume saving is largely not, and the import bill in domestic currency rises even though fewer units are bought. Expecting the volumes to respond as fast as the price is the single assumption that turns an improvement into a deterioration, and it is the assumption the data have to be read against.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.topic: A policy claim the model contradicts
questions.learningObjective: explain why a balanced-budget rule is not neutral in the expenditure model
questions.stem: A government argues that a balanced-budget rule cannot affect aggregate demand, because under the rule the increase in government purchases is exactly matched by the increase in taxes. Using the simple expenditure model with a marginal propensity to consume of 0.75 and a tax rate of 0.20, explain why the model predicts otherwise.

answer.exemplar: The two changes are not equally powerful per unit, so the balanced-budget multiplier is not zero but one. The spending multiplier is one over one minus c times one minus t, which is one over 0.4, that is 2.5, while the tax multiplier is minus c times one minus t over 0.4, which is minus 1.5. Applied to an equal rise of 20 billion in each, the spending adds 50 billion of demand and the taxes remove 30, so output rises by 20 billion and the deficit stays at zero. The intuition is that a tax increase destroys only the consumed part of the income it takes, since the remainder is saved, while a spending increase puts its whole amount into the circular flow. The claim in the rule that a pound of spending and a pound of tax are interchangeable is what the model rejects, and it is a claim about behaviour, so it is vulnerable to evidence about saving rather than to arithmetic.

questions.explanation: Compute both multipliers and add them; they are not equal in size.
questions.hint: The rule is not neutrality of the budget, it is neutrality of demand, and the two come apart. Under the rule the government does exactly as much spending and raises exactly as much tax, but a tax increase is not the mirror image of a spending increase: it removes only the part of income that is consumed and leaves the saved part alone, whereas a spending increase puts its whole amount into demand. Recognising that the two effects have different sizes is not an accounting nicety, because the size of the tax multiplier rests on the propensity to consume, which is a behavioural parameter. The claim being rejected is therefore an empirical one dressed as an identity, and the model's contribution is to show exactly which behaviour would have to hold for the claim to be true.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: explain how buying long-term bonds works when the policy rate is already at zero
questions.stem: A central bank has cut its policy rate to zero and short-term yields are at zero, but ten-year yields remain well above that. It announces large purchases of long-term government bonds. Explain how that can lower long-term rates and support spending when the usual policy channel is unavailable.

answer.exemplar: The usual channel runs through a rate the central bank sets, and at zero there is no room left to cut, so purchases have to work through expectations and through the price of the assets it buys. By committing to buy long-term bonds rather than short ones, the authority tells markets that it is willing to hold duration, and investors who expect the central bank to be slow to sell again demand less compensation for holding long risk, so the ten-year yield falls. Lower long-term yields reduce the discount rate applied to future income and cut the interest cost of long-lived investment, so projects that were not worth financing become worth financing. The mechanism also runs through expectations of the future policy rate: purchases credible enough to last are a statement that rates will stay low for a long time, and that statement is itself part of what lowers yields. The limitation is that this works only to the extent bonds are scarce, since a central bank cannot lower a price it is willing to buy without limit.

questions.explanation: Ask what changes when there is no room left to change the short rate.
questions.hint: The temptation is to conclude that once the policy rate is at zero the authority has run out of instruments, which confuses a floor on one rate with a floor on all of them. Long-term yields are set in a different market by a different set of holders, and nothing about a zero floor on overnight funds requires them to be at zero too. What links the two is the expectation that the short rate will stay low, and that expectation is precisely what a purchase of long-term paper commits the authority to. Saying the purchases do nothing because money is already cheap misses the difference between the stock of money and the price of duration, and saying they lower every rate ignores that a central bank cannot push a price below the level at which it is willing to keep buying.
